goal: Separate a sighting from a prediction.
jobs: Mark where to aim at minute 3. Tell the operator which dots were measured and which dot you predicted.
Give viewers a two-sentence update. Point to a measured dot, then say where you expect the next one.
first: Where should the camera look next? Use the timed dots in your call.
revised: Does the new sighting fit your prediction? Tell the next crew what to check.
honors: What new observation would make you change your prediction? Explain why.
frame: Aim at ___ because ___.

goal: Tell distance traveled and change in position apart.
jobs: Mark both parts of the route and draw one start-to-finish arrow. Report the trip length and change in position.
Guide a new driver to the finish. Give the trip length, change in position, and final location.
first: What numbers should dispatch use? Say what each number measures.
revised: Check the new location instruction. What should dispatch tell the driver now?
honors: If right becomes negative, which numbers change sign? Which quantities stay the same?
frame: The trip was ___. The finish is ___.

goal: Use a position-time graph to find velocity.
jobs: Calculate the signed average velocity. Mark the two sightings on the graph so the next operator can check your result.
Report a speed and direction. Tell viewers whether these two sightings show that XJ is slowing down.
first: What can you report about XJ's motion? Use the graph to support your call.
revised: Check the new caption. Write the correction you would send or say on air.
honors: What can these two sightings tell you about average velocity? What can they not tell you about motion between sightings?
frame: XJ moves ___ at an average of ___.

goal: Use signed graph areas to find displacement.
jobs: Shade both parts of the velocity graph. Radio the camera's final change in position, including direction.
Mark the outward and return shots. Report total distance and net movement to the editor.
first: Where does the camera finish relative to its start? How far did it travel?
revised: Check the new caption. Which number belongs on the location graphic? Explain.
honors: If the camera also moves sideways, why does that motion need its own velocity-time graph?
frame: The camera travels ___ but ends ___.

goal: Read forecast bounds without inventing a probability.
jobs: Label both search bands with their endpoints. Recommend which report needs a wider telescope search.
Present both forecast bands. Explain which search is wider and what the bands do not tell us about impact.
first: What search area should the crew prepare for? Use both sets of endpoints.
revised: Check the editor's new label. What can you report from these bands?
honors: How is changing an input's uncertainty different from changing how you expect XJ to move?
frame: Team ___ needs a wider search because ___.

goal: Combine two displacement components into one arrow.
jobs: Draw one arrow for the whole displacement. Give its length and direction, and label both component legs.
Use the map to report the whole movement. Explain why '7 km closer to Earth' is the wrong caption.
first: What full movement should the second telescope track? Use your map.
revised: What part can the updated tracker measure? What part will it miss?
honors: Give the direction as an angle. Name the line you measure that angle from.
frame: The whole displacement is ___ toward ___.

goal: Use a velocity change to find acceleration.
jobs: Radio the average acceleration with its sign and unit. Label both velocity arrows so the crew can check it.
Narrate the two-second change. Point to the arrow lengths to explain whether XJ sped up or slowed down.
first: Which speed alert should the control room use? Support it with the arrows.
revised: Check the proposed banner. Give a corrected report using the two velocities.
honors: Why do two velocity readings give an average acceleration rather than the acceleration at every instant?
frame: The speed ___ because the arrow ___.

goal: Use a velocity-time graph to predict displacement.
jobs: Shade the area under the velocity-time trace. Send the camera's displacement at the end of the shot.
Explain why using the final speed for the whole clip would miss the shot. Point to the graph as you speak.
first: Where should the camera look relative to the start? Show how the graph helps.
revised: Does the new report still let you guarantee that displacement? Explain your revised call.
honors: Check your first answer with a kinematics equation. What does that equation treat as constant?
frame: Our forecast is ___ if ___ stays constant.

goal: Use timed sightings to make a prediction, then check it.
jobs: Radio a camera window. Point to the sightings that support your call.
Give a 15-second update. Use your cart drawing to explain why XJ can keep moving without an engine.
first: Where should the camera look? Why?
revised: What will you tell them now? Use the new sighting in your update.
honors: Why could a straight-line forecast work for a minute even while gravity pulls on XJ?
frame: Aim at ___ because ___.

goal: Name the source and receiver of each force.
jobs: Approve the force layer for XJ. Name who exerts each force and what receives it. Keep motion separate.
Prepare the viewer graphic. Ask your partner who causes each proposed force before you approve its label.
first: Which force arrows should go live? Explain each arrow you keep or remove.
revised: Does the new information change the force layer? Explain your update.
honors: Name another real source of force on XJ. Where would its arrow go, and what would you label it?
frame: Keep ___ because ___ acts on ___.

goal: Compare velocity changes when masses differ.
jobs: Compare the two test runs. Tell the crew which body changes velocity more and use the masses to explain why.
Explain why equal pushes can give different results. Have your partner check what stayed the same in both tests.
first: Which body changes velocity more? Explain your first call from the test card.
revised: What changed in the test? Give the crew a new comparison.
honors: Check both runs using mass times acceleration. Do your results match the forces on the test card?
frame: Run ___ changes more because ___.

goal: Compare velocity changes when net forces differ.
jobs: Add velocity-change arrows for both runs. Recommend the larger change and name what stayed the same.
Tell viewers which run changes velocity more. Ask whether doubling motor pull always doubles the net force.
first: How do the two velocity changes compare? Point to the force arrows.
revised: Do the new readings still support your comparison? Explain what you must check.
honors: Explain the difference between doubling one applied force and doubling the net force.
frame: The velocity change is ___ if ___ stays the same.

goal: Distinguish motion, net force, and acceleration.
jobs: Draw the net-force and acceleration arrows. Tell the operator what happens to speed while the body still moves left.
Label separate arrows for motion and acceleration. Explain to viewers how they can point opposite ways.
first: What happens to speed at first? Include the net force and acceleration in your call.
revised: Check the updated display. What does a force arrow tell you, and what does it not tell you?
honors: What additional information would let you predict when the body stops and reverses?
frame: It moves ___ while acceleration points ___.

goal: Place an interaction pair on its two receivers.
jobs: Put each gravitational arrow on the body that receives it. Send the animator two corrected object panels.
Write a split-screen caption naming who pulls whom. Explain why equal force does not require equal acceleration.
first: Do the two arrows cancel on XJ? Explain using your corrected panels.
revised: Which arrow belongs in the updated shot? Name its source and receiver.
honors: If Earth and XJ are one combined system, which forces in this interaction are internal to that system?
frame: ___ pulls on ___. That arrow belongs on ___.

goal: Keep only forces on the chosen object in its diagram.
jobs: Outline XJ as the chosen object. Keep only the force arrows you would use to calculate XJ's acceleration.
Separate the force and motion layers. Tell the animator which Earth arrow belongs in a different shot.
first: Which arrows belong in 'forces on XJ'? Explain what you keep and move.
revised: Where does the new arrow belong? Update the force layer and explain.
honors: Must XJ move in the direction of its net force? Give a possible motion that shows your reasoning.
frame: This arrow acts on ___, so it belongs ___.

goal: Represent one force without counting it twice.
jobs: Prepare the component view for the calculator. Mark the full-force arrow that these components replace.
Show the full force and its component view. Write a caption that prevents counting the same pull twice.
first: Which arrows should enter the force sum? Explain your choice.
revised: Check the calculator request. What correction would you send before it runs?
honors: If XJ's velocity points horizontally, which force component changes its speed at that instant? Why?
frame: Use ___ because the components represent ___.

goal: Use contact surfaces to decide when friction acts.
jobs: Set friction for each scene. Mark the touching surfaces and explain what could change XJ's motion in empty space.
Correct the caption for the two shots. Point to the surfaces and say what could still bend XJ's path.
first: What should the two-scene caption say? Explain using the contact surfaces.
revised: What changed in the new shot? Update the force explanation for XJ.
honors: How would entering an atmosphere change the forces you include? Explain where the added force comes from.
frame: In this scene, ___ touches ___, so ___.

goal: Distinguish zero acceleration from zero velocity.
jobs: Choose the status graphic. Mark where XJ should be two seconds later relative to the first sighting.
Choose the on-air label. Explain why zero acceleration and zero speed do not mean the same thing.
first: Which status should go live? Use a second position to support your call.
revised: Can the old status describe the next interval? Explain what the new report changes.
honors: In two dimensions, what must the force sums be along both axes for the forces to balance?
frame: The status is ___ because net force ___.

goal: Use all forces to calculate acceleration.
jobs: Mark the first wrong calculator step. Send the developer the corrected force sum and expected acceleration.
Stop or clear the graphic. Give the anchor a corrected number that viewers can check against the force arrows.
first: Can this calculation go live? Give the corrected result and explain.
revised: Did the developer fix the error? Send a follow-up that names what still needs changing.
honors: Create a different pair of opposing forces that would expose the same calculator error. Show the correct result.
frame: The force sum is ___, so acceleration is ___.

goal: Identify which measurements a position forecast needs.
jobs: Mark what you can calculate now. Send the telescope operator a request for the measurements still needed.
Prepare a 'known / still needed' graphic. Tell the anchor which result can air and which must wait.
first: What can the desk release now? What measurements must the crew still collect?
revised: Is the forecast ready after the update? Say what you can release and what is still missing.
honors: If XJ reverses direction during the forecast, how would that affect a report of distance versus displacement?
frame: We can find ___. We still need ___.

goal: Compare position reports that use different zeros.
jobs: Use one axis for both stations. Give dispatch the position from A, then name what a future forecast still needs.
Show both stations and zeros on the locator map. Explain whether the two reports describe different locations.
first: Do the reports agree? Give one location and explain how the map supports it.
revised: What number changes in the new frame? What physical location stays the same?
honors: What measurement uncertainty should accompany a future central position forecast? Give a concrete example.
frame: From station ___, the position is ___.

goal: Compare forecast ranges and keep conclusions within the data.
jobs: Mark both forecast bands. Issue a location bulletin and name an observation that would trigger another update.
Decide whether to air the headline. Show both intervals and write the replacement line viewers should hear.
first: What location can you report? Should the proposed headline air? Explain.
revised: Answer the caller using the bands. What can your desk report, and what is still unknown?
honors: How is predicting XJ's location different from deciding what action people should take?
frame: The ranges show ___. They do not show ___.
